claims.text: What the image looks like Hyperdense MCA sign, loss of gray-white differentiation, insular ribbon sign, sulcal effacement → acute ischemic stroke (early CT signs < 6 h)
claims.quote: Hyperdense MCA sign, loss of gray-white differentiation, insular ribbon sign, sulcal effacement Acute ischemic stroke (early CT signs <6 h)

claims.text: CT evidence of even a large anterior circulation stroke may be subtle during the first few hours; changes may include effacement of sulci or the insular cortical ribbon, loss of the gray-white junction, and a dense middle cerebral artery sign
claims.quote: CT evidence of even a large anterior circulation ischemic stroke may be subtle during the first few hours; changes may include effacement of sulci or the insular cortical ribbon, loss of the gray-white junction between cortex and white matter, and a dense middle cerebral artery sign.

claims.text: CT or MRI is done first to exclude intracerebral hemorrhage, subdural or epidural hematoma, and a rapidly growing, bleeding or suddenly symptomatic tumor
claims.quote: Neuroimaging with CT or MRI is performed first to exclude intracerebral hemorrhage, subdural or epidural hematoma, and a rapidly growing, bleeding, or suddenly symptomatic tumor.

claims.text: Causes Common causes: atherothrombotic occlusion of large arteries; cerebral embolism (embolic infarction); nonthrombotic occlusion of small, deep cerebral arteries (lacunar infarction); proximal arterial stenosis with hypotension reducing flow in watershed zones (hemodynamic stroke); no cause is identified in one-third at discharge (cryptogenic)
claims.quote: Common causes are atherothrombotic occlusion of large arteries; cerebral embolism (embolic infarction); nonthrombotic occlusion of small, deep cerebral arteries (lacunar infarction); and proximal arterial stenosis with hypotension that decreases cerebral blood flow in arterial watershed zones (hemodynamic stroke). No cause is identified in one-third of ischemic strokes at the time of patient discharge; these strokes are categorized as cryptogenic.

claims.text: Symptoms Symptoms depend on the part of the brain affected; deficit patterns often suggest the affected artery, but correlation is often inexact
claims.quote: Symptoms and signs of ischemic stroke depend on the part of brain affected. Patterns of neurologic deficits often suggest the affected artery (see table ), but correlation is often inexact.

claims.text: Middle cerebral artery (common): contralateral hemiparesis (worse in the arm and face than the leg), dysarthria, hemianesthesia, contralateral homonymous hemianopia, aphasia (dominant hemisphere) or apraxia and sensory neglect (nondominant hemisphere)
claims.quote: Contralateral hemiparesis (worse in the arm and face than in the leg), dysarthria, hemianesthesia, contralateral homonymous hemianopia, aphasia (if the dominant hemisphere is affected) or apraxia and sensory neglect (if the nondominant hemisphere is affected) | Middle cerebral artery (common)

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: tPA if <4.5 h and no contraindications; thrombectomy if LVO <24 h
claims.quote: tPA if <4.5 h and no contraindications; thrombectomy if LVO <24 h

claims.text: Recombinant tPA (alteplase) can be used up to 3 hours after onset if there are no contraindications; some experts recommend up to 4.5 hours, with additional exclusion criteria between 3 and 4.5 hours; tPA must be given within 4.5 hours, timed from when the patient was last observed to be well
claims.quote: Recombinant tPA (alteplase) can be used for patients with acute ischemic stroke up to 3 hours after symptom onset if they have no contraindications to tPA (see table ). Some experts recommend using tPA up to 4.5 hours after symptom onset (see Expansion of the Time Window for Treatment of Acute Ischemic Stroke With Intravenous Tissue Plasminogen Activator); however, between 3 hours and 4.5 hours after symptom onset, additional exclusion criteria apply (see table ). Thus, tPA must be given within 4.5 hours of symptom onset—a difficult requirement. Because the precise time of symptom onset may not be known, clinicians must start timing from the moment the patient was last observed to be well.

claims.text: tPA dose 0.9 mg/kg IV (maximum 90 mg): 10% by rapid IV injection over 1 minute, the rest over 60 minutes; anticoagulants and antiplatelets are not used within 24 hours of tPA
claims.quote: Dose of tPA is 0.9 mg/kg IV (maximum dose 90 mg); 10% is given by rapid IV injection over 1 minute, and the remainder by constant infusion over 60 minutes. Vital signs are closely monitored for 24 hours after treatment. Any bleeding complications are aggressively managed. Anticoagulants and antiplatelet medications are not used within 24 hours of treatment with tPA.

claims.text: Guidelines recommend vessel imaging (CTA or MRA) for all patients with suspected large vessel occlusion, especially within 24 hours of onset
claims.quote: Guidelines recommend that all patients with clinical suspicion of large vessel occlusion should undergo vessel imaging (CTA or MRA), especially within 24 hours of symptom onset given advances in acute stroke treatment.

claims.text: Mechanical thrombectomy is standard of care in large stroke centers for recent large-vessel occlusion in the anterior circulation
claims.quote: Mechanical thrombectomy (angiographically directed intra-arterial removal of a thrombus or embolus by a stent retriever device) is standard of care in large stroke centers for patients with recent large-vessel occlusion in the anterior circulation.

claims.text: Thrombectomy was previously restricted to within 6 hours of onset (internal carotid or middle cerebral artery occlusion); later treatment may be justified at comprehensive stroke centers when clinical and/or imaging findings suggest substantial tissue at risk (penumbra): benefit up to 16 hours in DEFUSE 3 (small infarct, larger penumbra) and up to 24 hours in DAWN (large mismatch between infarct volume and clinical deficit)
claims.quote: Mechanical thrombectomy had previously been restricted to use within 6 hours of symptom onset in patients with internal carotid artery or middle cerebral artery occlusion. However, later treatment may be justified at comprehensive stroke centers when clinical and/or imaging findings that suggest presence of a substantial amount of tissue at risk of infarction (penumbra). The volume of infarcted tissue and at-risk underperfused tissue (ischemic penumbra) can be identified using perfusion CT or perfusion MRI. A sizeable mismatch between the infarct and at-risk volume identified by diffusion-weighted or perfusion-weighted imaging suggests that substantial penumbra is still potentially salvageable. In the DEFUSE 3 trial, benefit was evident up to 16 hours after symptom onset in patients with a small infarct and a larger penumbra; both findings are based on imaging criteria (7). In the DAWN trial, benefit was evident up to 24 hours after symptom onset in patients with a large mismatch between infarct volume based on imaging and severity of the clinical deficit based on clinical criteria (8).

claims.text: For large vessel occlusion, IV thrombolysis before thrombectomy is recommended when its criteria are met and should not be omitted in favor of thrombectomy alone
claims.quote: For patients with acute ischemic stroke due to emergent large vessel occlusion, administering intravenous thrombolysis before mechanical thrombectomy is recommended when criteria for intravenous thrombolysis are met, and intravenous thrombolysis should not be omitted in favor of mechanical thrombectomy alone (10).

claims.text: In general, do not aggressively reduce BP soon after acute ischemic stroke
claims.quote: In general, do not aggressively reduce BP soon after acute ischemic stroke.
